progression.prerequisiteKnowledge: From bio-m5-b01: sexual reproduction mixes two parents' alleles; offspring vary. From bio-m5-b02a: sperm must reach an egg; fertilisation. From bio-m5-b02b: anthers make pollen, a stigma receives it, a pollen tube carries sperm to the egg; many flowers can pollinate themselves; bags keep pollen out. From bio-m5-b03b: the steps of artificial insemination (semen collected, divided, usually frozen, placed in the uterus during heat) and of artificial pollination (remove the seed parent's anthers, place chosen pollen, keep other pollen out, for example with a bag); a few parents used widely narrow the gene pool. From bio-m5 meiosis (B7): each gamete gets one of each chromosome pair, with independent assortment and crossing over, so gametes differ. From b08: gene pool, drift (stronger in small populations), gene flow. From b09: reproductive technologies choose the parents and change no DNA (lane 2). From b12 and b13: the banana problem; weighing. Not assumed: comparing the two methods feature by feature, sex-sorted semen, hybrid seed fields, why a large herd can behave like a small population, writing a compare.
progression.startsWith: Choose parents whose gametes will meet. The video opens: One champion dairy bull can father tens of thousands of calves, across many countries, without ever meeting a cow.
progression.stopsAfter: explaining what both methods share (they choose which parents breed, change no DNA, and give offspring that still vary, because meiosis gives each gamete its own mix, so they make outcomes more likely, not certain); comparing their processes feature by feature (semen collected, checked, diluted into many doses and frozen for decades, against pollen collected from anthers and, for many crops, used fresh within hours; the cow inseminated during heat with no bull present, against the seed flower's anthers removed before they shed pollen, the flower protected from stray pollen until the chosen pollen is applied, and other pollen kept out while the cross is made, a bag being one way to isolate it); comparing their outcomes (both give offspring of the chosen parents; frozen semen gives one male a far greater reach, while pollination is usually flower by flower, though hybrid seed fields scale it up); explaining why heavy use of a few sires makes a large herd behave like a small population (chance losses, rising relatedness, recessive alleles pairing up) and that the cause is the breeding choice, not the method (many or imported sires add alleles; embryo transfer from a few prize cows narrows from the mothers' side; one variety planted everywhere narrows a crop); writing a compare one feature at a time; applying this to an unseen compare item and an unseen analyse item.
progression.nextLesson: copying instead of choosing: how a whole organism is cloned, and how that differs from cloning a gene (route entry bio-m6-b16, which merges b16 and b17).

teaching.task: Artificial insemination and artificial pollination both let a breeder choose which parents' gametes meet. So how do their steps and outcomes compare, and why can one of them reshape a whole breed so much faster?
teaching.causalExplanation: Causes: why offspring still vary (each gamete gets its own mix in meiosis, 2); why sorting does not give certainty (sorting is imperfect and fertilisation still involves chance, 2); why semen reaches further (freezing lets it keep and travel, 3 and 5); why a flower needs two blocking steps (pollen can arrive from its own anthers and from elsewhere, 4); why the cow needs only timing (no bull, no other sperm, 4); why a big herd can behave like a small one (few fathers, 6); why recessive disorders rise (relatedness pairs up recessive alleles, 6); why the method is not the cause (the same method can add alleles by gene flow, 7). Visible case: one board, two columns, a row per feature. Video advantage: the four gametes sending different ring sets; the reach map filling; the five-bull fan collapsing the ring cluster; the wind wisp bouncing off the bag. Thinking opportunities: two unseen items. Reading load: at most about three bright text items; the attempt 2 card with its table is the densest frame and is the task.
teaching.conversationalApproach: One bull can father tens of thousands of calves while a wheat breeder crosses plants one ear at a time, so the question is how artificial insemination and artificial pollination compare in their steps and outcomes; both choose the parents and change no DNA, and meiosis still gives each gamete its own mix, so they make an outcome more likely, not certain; the comparison board then adds one feature row at a time: collect and store (frozen semen keeps for decades, many crops' pollen lasts hours), deliver and keep other gametes out (timing with no bull present, against removing the seed flower's anthers and protecting it from stray pollen until the chosen pollen is applied, a bag being one way), reach (frozen semen against flower by flower, with hybrid seed fields), and the gene pool (five bulls make ten thousand cows behave like a small population), with the cause placed in the breeding choice, not the method. A compare is written one feature at a time. Two exam questions follow with brief feedback.
teaching.openingDecision: One champion dairy bull can father tens of thousands of calves, across many countries, without ever meeting a cow. A wheat breeder crosses her chosen plants one ear at a time. Both are choosing which parents' gametes meet. So how do artificial insemination and artificial pollination compare, in their steps and in their outcomes? And why can one of them reshape a whole breed so much faster?
teaching.understandingCheck: 10a is a compare item: a tomato breeder (tomatoes usually pollinate themselves) and a cattle breeder whose chosen bull is in another state; compare the processes each would use so that only the chosen father's gametes take part. It tests the syllabus verb on the process features, with new species. 10c is an analyse item: hypothetical breed data (cow numbers steady over forty years, bulls fathering calves falling sharply, a recessive disorder rising); analyse how artificial insemination could explain the data and suggest one change. It tests the gene pool outcome on new evidence. Each ends "Pause here to answer." with a 10 s countdown; the full card stays on screen during and after the countdown. Each feedback is brief (about 25 to 30 s): answer, key reasons, the givens underlined in the question strip as they are used, one crossed-out classic mistake. No givens card.
teaching.curriculumScope: B6-IQ3-02: "compare the processes and outcomes of reproductive technologies, including but not limited to:" with its two listed examples, "artificial insemination" and "artificial pollination". This video owns full coverage of B6-IQ3-02. B6-IQ3-01: "investigate the uses and advantages of current genetic technologies that induce genetic change": b09 took the framing; this video completes it for the two reproductive technologies (uses: spreading chosen traits, planned crosses, hybrid seed; advantages: reach, storage, speed, no need to move animals; limits: probability not certainty, narrowing). Update the ledger rows when this design passes review. The verbs: "compare" is carried by scenes 3 to 5, scene 8 and attempt 1 (what-markers-reward: "Compare: deal with the same feature on both sides, then cover the features requested. ... In a 2025 task, a complete comparison of artificial insemination and pollination reached three marks; an incomplete comparison reached two."). Attempt 2 uses "analyse" (what-markers-reward: "break down the evidence or process and show relationships to the question's claim or outcome").

design.visualSystem: One comparison board throughout: two columns, "artificial insemination" (left, headed by `b3b-dairy-bull-side-v1.png`) and "artificial pollination" (right, headed by `b3b-wheat-ear-floret-v1.png`, the ear half), and feature rows that are added one per scene, each with a small grey label: "what both do" (scene 2, a merged row across both columns), "collect and store" (scene 3), "deliver, and keep other gametes out" (scene 4), "reach" (scene 5), "effect on the gene pool" (scenes 6 and 7). Each cell holds a painted object or coded action, never a paragraph; a short grey chip names the feature, and the bright item is always the cell being spoken about. Animal side: `m6-insemination-straw-tank-v1.png` (dewar and straw), `b3b-straw-frost-v1.png`, `b3b-cow-tract-v1.png` (anatomy diagram only; a coded thin tube enters through the cervix to the uterus; no animal body, no person, no hands), `b3b-dairy-cow-side-v1.png` and `b3b-calf-side-v1.png` (calf glyph rows). Plant side: `b3b-wheat-ear-floret-v1.png` (floret half), `b3b-forceps-v1.png` (shown lifting anthers by coded motion, no hand), `b3b-cover-bag-v1.png`, `b2b-paintbrush-pollination-v1.png` (brush on a stigma, no hand), and the new `m6-maize-hybrid-rows-v1.png`. Cells: `cd-four-cells-v1.png` (four gametes from one parent, from the brief 88 cell set) for meiosis; X and Y sperm in scene 2 are coded slim sperm glyphs with a small chromosome letter on screen only, never painted over a cell. Gene pool: b08's and b12's ring clusters (coloured rings, no letters), with a coded pedigree fan (five father glyphs, many calf glyphs) in scene 6. Never used: `m6-hand-pollination-v1.png` and `m6-agricultural-liming-v1.png` (hands). No people, no hands. Clutter rule (owner, 19 Oct): at most about three bright text items at once besides the small grey row labels; each chip dims when the next cue lands; the column not being spoken about dims to grey.
